1:1.t: "The record of the ancestry": the KJV's "The book of the generation", the same phrase as Genesis 2:4 and 5:1.
"Christ" (Greek christos): "anointed one", the Greek translation of the Hebrew mashiach, Messiah. It is a title before it becomes a name. In Matthew it is often "the Christ", the promised King.

1:2.t: Names follow their Old Testament spelling (Judah, Perez, Boaz, Uzziah) rather than the Greek forms the KJV uses here (Judas, Phares, Booz, Ozias).

1:3.t: Matthew includes four women: Tamar, Rahab, Ruth and the wife of Uriah (Bathsheba), outsiders and people with irregular stories, all part of the line of the Messiah.

1:5.t: Matthew includes four women: Tamar, Rahab, Ruth and the wife of Uriah (Bathsheba), outsiders and people with irregular stories, all part of the line of the Messiah.

1:6.t: Matthew includes four women: Tamar, Rahab, Ruth and the wife of Uriah (Bathsheba), outsiders and people with irregular stories, all part of the line of the Messiah.

1:8.t: Matthew passes over three kings between Jehoram and Uzziah (2 Kings 8-14). Genealogies often skipped generations.

1:18.t: "Pledged to be married": the KJV's "espoused". Betrothal was a binding agreement that could be ended only by divorce.
"The Holy Spirit": the KJV's "the Holy Ghost". "Ghost" in older English meant "spirit".

1:20.t: "The Holy Spirit": the KJV's "the Holy Ghost". "Ghost" in older English meant "spirit".

1:25.t: "Did not have marital relations with her": the KJV's "knew her not".

2:1.t: Herod the Great died in 4 BC, so Jesus was born a few years before that.
"Wise men": Greek magoi, scholars from Persia or Babylonia who studied the stars. Matthew does not say there were three; three gifts are named.

2:4.t: "Teachers of the law": the KJV's "scribes", experts in the law of Moses.

2:6.t: A quotation of Micah 5:2, with 2 Samuel 5:2.

2:22.t: Archelaus, a son of Herod, ruled Judea from 4 BC to AD 6 and was notorious for cruelty.

3:4.t: Locusts were permitted food (Leviticus 11:22). John's clothing recalled Elijah (2 Kings 1:8).

3:7.t: Pharisees were strict keepers of the law and its traditions; Sadducees were the priestly party, who accepted only the five books of Moses and denied the resurrection.

4:4.t: Jesus answers each temptation from Deuteronomy (8:3, 6:16, 6:13).

4:7.t: Jesus answers each temptation from Deuteronomy (8:3, 6:16, 6:13).

4:10.t: Jesus answers each temptation from Deuteronomy (8:3, 6:16, 6:13).

4:19.t: "Fishers of people": the KJV's "fishers of men"; the Greek anthropoi means people in general.

4:24.t: "Possessed by demons": the KJV's "possessed with devils". The Greek daimonion means a demon, an evil spirit; "devil" (diabolos) is reserved for Satan. "Having seizures": the KJV's "lunatick", from a word meaning "moonstruck".

4:25.t: The Decapolis ("ten cities") was a region of Greek cities east of the Jordan.

5:15.t: "A basket": the KJV's "a bushel", a grain basket.

5:18.t: "The smallest letter ... the least stroke of a pen": the KJV's "one jot or one tittle". The jot is yod, the smallest Hebrew letter; a tittle is a tiny stroke that distinguishes one letter from another.

5:22.t: "Without cause": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts do not have these words. "Raca": an Aramaic insult meaning "empty-head". "The court": the KJV's "the council", the Sanhedrin.
"Brother or sister": the KJV's "brother". The Greek adelphos, used of fellow believers, includes women and men.

"Hell" (Greek geenna): Gehenna, from the Hebrew Ge-Hinnom, the Valley of Hinnom south of Jerusalem, where children had once been burned to Molech (Jeremiah 7:31). It became the name for the place of final judgment. The KJV also uses "hell" for Hades (the realm of the dead, 16:18) and Tartarus (2 Peter 2:4); this translation notes which word is meant.

5:26.t: "The last penny": the KJV's "the uttermost farthing"; Greek kodrantes, the smallest Roman coin, a sixty-fourth of a denarius.

5:40.t: "Shirt ... coat": the KJV's "coat ... cloke", the inner tunic and outer cloak. The outer cloak could not be kept overnight as a pledge (Exodus 22:26).

5:41.t: "About one and a half kilometers": the KJV's "a mile", a Roman mile of a thousand paces. Roman soldiers could force civilians to carry their gear that far.

5:44.t: "Bless those who curse you, do good to those who hate you ... mistreat you": the KJV's reading; some early manuscripts have only "love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you".

5:46.t: "Tax collectors": the KJV's "publicans", local Jews who collected taxes for Rome and were despised as collaborators.

6:1.t: "Your giving to the needy": the KJV's "your alms". Some manuscripts read "your righteousness".

6:4.t: "Openly": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts do not have this word.

6:6.t: "Openly": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts do not have this word.

6:18.t: "Openly": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts do not have this word.

6:13.t: "For Yours is the kingdom and the power and the glory forever. Amen.": the KJV's reading. Many early manuscripts end the prayer at "deliver us from evil"; the closing words were likely added for use in worship (compare 1 Chronicles 29:11). "From evil" can also be read "from the evil one".

6:24.t: "Money": the KJV's "mammon", an Aramaic word for wealth or possessions.

6:27.t: "About half a meter": the KJV's "one cubit". The Greek helikia can mean height or length of life, so many read "add a single hour to your life".

6:28.t: "Flowers": the KJV's "lilies", probably wildflowers in general.

6:30.t: "Into the fire": the KJV's "into the oven". Dried grass was burned as fuel.

7:3.t: "Speck ... plank": the KJV's "mote ... beam", a splinter and a roof beam.

7:29.t: "The teachers of the law": the KJV's "the scribes"; many manuscripts read "their teachers of the law".

8:2.t: "Leprosy": the Greek lepra covered various skin diseases, not only Hansen's disease. Such people were ceremonially unclean (Leviticus 13-14).

8:5.t: A centurion was a Roman officer in command of about a hundred soldiers.

8:19.t: "A teacher of the law": the KJV's "a certain scribe". "Teacher": the KJV's "Master", Greek didaskalos.

8:28.t: "Gergesenes": the KJV's reading; many manuscripts read "Gadarenes", others "Gerasenes". All refer to the area southeast of the Sea of Galilee.

9:2.t: "Mat": the KJV's "bed", a sleeping mat or stretcher.

9:9.t: "The tax collector's booth": the KJV's "the receipt of custom". Matthew is called Levi in Mark 2:14 and Luke 5:27.

9:13.t: A quotation of Hosea 6:6. "To repentance": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts do not have these words.
"Mercy" (Greek eleos): in Hosea 6:6 the Hebrew is hesed, steadfast love and loyalty. God values faithful love over ritual.

9:17.t: "Wineskins": the KJV's "bottles", containers made of animal skins.

9:18.t: "A synagogue leader": the KJV's "a certain ruler"; Mark 5:22 names him Jairus.

10:3.t: "Lebbaeus, who was called Thaddaeus": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts have only "Thaddaeus". Luke 6:16 calls him Judas son of James.

10:4.t: "Simon the Zealot": the KJV's "Simon the Canaanite", from the Aramaic qan'an, "zealous", not the land of Canaan. Zealots were nationalists opposed to Rome.

10:8.t: "Raise the dead": the KJV's reading; some manuscripts do not have these words.

10:9.t: "Belts": the KJV's "purses". Money was carried in a fold of the belt.

10:10.t: "Bag": the KJV's "scrip", a traveler's or beggar's bag.

10:25.t: "Beelzebub": a name for the prince of demons, perhaps from Baal-Zebub, "lord of the flies" (2 Kings 1:2).

10:29.t: "A penny": the KJV's "a farthing"; Greek assarion, a small copper coin, a sixteenth of a denarius.

11:14.t: "Elijah": the KJV's "Elias", the Greek form. Malachi 4:5 promised that God would send the prophet Elijah before the day of the LORD; Jesus says John the Baptist fulfills that promise.

11:19.t: "Children": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts read "deeds".

11:21.t: Chorazin and Bethsaida were towns near Capernaum on the north shore of the Sea of Galilee.

12:1.t: "Grainfields": the KJV's "the corn"; in 1611 "corn" meant grain, here wheat or barley. Picking grain by hand from a neighbor's field was allowed (Deuteronomy 23:25); the Pharisees objected to doing it on the Sabbath.

12:4.t: "The consecrated bread": the KJV's "the shewbread", the bread of the Presence (1 Samuel 21:1-6, Leviticus 24:5-9).

12:6.t: "Something greater": the KJV's "one greater". The Greek is neuter, "something greater".

12:40.t: "A huge fish": the KJV's "the whale"; Greek ketos, a sea creature. Jonah 1:17 says "a great fish".
"Three days and three nights": a Jewish way of counting any part of a day as a day. Jesus died on Friday and rose on Sunday, the third day (16:21).

12:42.t: The Queen of the South is the queen of Sheba (1 Kings 10:1-13).

12:46.t: Jesus' brothers are named in 13:55. Christians differ on whether they were Mary's later children, Joseph's children from an earlier marriage, or cousins.

12:47.t: Some early manuscripts do not have this verse.

13:25.t: "Weeds": the KJV's "tares", probably darnel, a weed that looks like wheat until it heads out.

13:32.t: "The smallest of all seeds": the smallest seed commonly sown in Palestine; it grows into a shrub up to about three meters tall.

13:33.t: "About 22 liters of flour": the KJV's "three measures of meal". The measure (Greek saton, Hebrew seah) held about 7.3 liters, so three made enough bread for about a hundred people.

13:35.t: A quotation of Psalm 78:2, by Asaph, who is called a seer (2 Chronicles 29:30).

13:39.t: "The end of the age": the KJV's "the end of the world"; Greek aion, age.

13:40.t: "The end of the age": the KJV's "the end of the world"; Greek aion, age.

13:49.t: "The end of the age": the KJV's "the end of the world"; Greek aion, age.

13:55.t: "Joses": the KJV's reading; many manuscripts read "Joseph". "Carpenter": Greek tekton, a builder who worked in wood or stone.

14:1.t: Herod the tetrarch: Herod Antipas, son of Herod the Great, ruler of Galilee and Perea. A tetrarch ruled part of a divided kingdom.

14:3.t: Herodias had left her husband Philip, Antipas's half-brother, to marry Antipas, a marriage the law forbade (Leviticus 18:16).

14:6.t: The daughter of Herodias is named Salome by the historian Josephus.

14:25.t: "Shortly before dawn": the KJV's "the fourth watch of the night", from about three to six in the morning.

14:34.t: Gennesaret was a fertile plain on the northwest shore of the Sea of Galilee.

15:2.t: The tradition of the elders required ritual hand-washing before meals, a matter of ceremonial purity, not hygiene.

15:5.t: "Devoted to God": the KJV's "It is a gift". Mark 7:11 gives the word Corban. By declaring property dedicated to God, a son could avoid supporting his parents.

15:8.t: A quotation of Isaiah 29:13 from the Greek.

15:17.t: "Out of the body": the KJV's "cast out into the draught", the latrine.

15:39.t: "Magdala": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts read "Magadan".

16:2.t: Some early manuscripts do not have the words from "When evening comes" to the end of verse 3.

16:13.t: Caesarea Philippi was a city at the foot of Mount Hermon, about 40 kilometers north of the Sea of Galilee.

16:17.t: "Son of Jonah": the KJV's "Bar-jona", Aramaic for "son of Jonah". John 1:42 gives the father's name as John.

17:4.t: "Shelters": the KJV's "tabernacles", booths like those made for the Festival of Tabernacles.

17:15.t: "He has seizures": the KJV's "he is lunatick", "moonstruck".

17:21.t: The KJV includes this verse; many early manuscripts do not have it. Compare Mark 9:29.

17:24.t: "The two-drachma temple tax": the KJV's "tribute money"; Greek didrachma, the yearly half-shekel tax every Jewish man paid for the temple (Exodus 30:13-16), about two days' pay.

17:27.t: "A four-drachma coin": the KJV's "a piece of money"; Greek stater, enough to pay the tax for two people.

18:11.t: The KJV includes this verse; many early manuscripts do not have it. Compare Luke 19:10.

18:22.t: "Seventy times seven": the KJV's reading; the Greek can also mean "seventy-seven times" (compare Genesis 4:24). Either way, forgiveness without limit.

18:24.t: "Ten thousand talents": in New Testament times a talent was a sum of money, about six thousand denarii, or twenty years' wages for a laborer (a weight of about 34 kilograms of silver). The debt was beyond any hope of repayment.

18:28.t: "A hundred denarii": the KJV's "an hundred pence". A denarius was a day's pay, so the debt was about a hundred days' wages.

19:9.t: "And whoever marries a divorced woman commits adultery": the KJV's reading; some early manuscripts do not have these words.

19:12.t: "Choose to live like eunuchs": the KJV's "made themselves eunuchs", meaning those who stay unmarried to serve the kingdom.

19:17.t: "Why do you call Me good? No one is good except One, that is, God": the KJV's reading. Many early manuscripts read "Why do you ask Me about what is good? There is only One who is good."

20:2.t: "A denarius": the KJV's "a penny", a Roman silver coin, the usual day's wage for a laborer.

20:3.t: "About nine in the morning ... noon ... three in the afternoon ... five in the afternoon": the KJV's "the third ... sixth ... ninth ... eleventh hour", counting from sunrise.

20:16.t: "For many are called, but few are chosen": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts do not have these words here (compare 22:14).

20:22.t: "And be baptized with the baptism I am baptized with": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts do not have these words here (compare Mark 10:38-39).

21:1.t: Bethphage was a village on the Mount of Olives, near Bethany.

21:5.t: A quotation of Zechariah 9:9, with Isaiah 62:11.

21:16.t: A quotation of Psalm 8:2 from the Greek.

21:33.t: "Farmers ... tenants": the KJV's "husbandmen". The parable echoes Isaiah 5:1-7.

21:42.t: "Cornerstone" (Greek kephale gonias): the KJV's "the head of the corner", the main stone that holds two walls together, or the capstone. See also Acts 4:11 and 1 Peter 2:7.

21:44.t: Some early manuscripts do not have this verse.

22:16.t: The Herodians were supporters of Herod's family and so of Roman rule; the Pharisees opposed the tax. A yes or no would offend one side or the other.

22:17.t: "The imperial tax": the KJV's "tribute", a yearly poll tax paid to Rome.

22:19.t: "A denarius": the KJV's "a penny", bearing the emperor's portrait and title.

22:35.t: "An expert in the law": the KJV's "a lawyer", a teacher of the law of Moses.

22:37.t: A quotation of Deuteronomy 6:5. 22:39 quotes Leviticus 19:18.
"Mind" (Greek dianoia): Deuteronomy 6:5 reads "strength". Mark 12:30 lists heart, soul, mind and strength. The Hebrew idea is love with the whole person.

23:5.t: "Phylacteries": small leather boxes containing verses of Scripture, worn on the forehead and arm (Deuteronomy 6:8). "Tassels": the KJV's "the borders", the fringes commanded in Numbers 15:38-39.

23:10.t: "Instructors": the KJV's "masters"; Greek kathegetes, a teacher or guide.

23:14.t: The KJV includes this verse; many early manuscripts do not have it. Compare Mark 12:40 and Luke 20:47.

23:23.t: "Faithfulness" (Greek pistis): usually "faith", but here, beside justice and mercy, it means faithfulness or loyalty, echoing Micah 6:8.

23:24.t: Pharisees strained their drinks to avoid swallowing an unclean insect (Leviticus 11:41-43); a camel was also unclean.

23:27.t: Tombs were whitewashed so that people would not touch them by accident and become unclean (Numbers 19:16).

23:35.t: Abel is the first murder in the Bible (Genesis 4:8) and Zechariah the last in the Hebrew Bible's order, which ends with Chronicles (2 Chronicles 24:20-21). There Zechariah is the son of Jehoiada, perhaps his grandfather.

24:3.t: "The end of the age": the KJV's "the end of the world"; Greek aion. Also 13:39.
"Coming" (Greek parousia): arrival or presence, used of a king's official visit. It became the term for Christ's return.

24:15.t: "The abomination that causes desolation" (Greek to bdelygma tes eremoseos): a desecration of the temple. Antiochus IV set up a pagan altar there in 167 BC (Daniel 11:31); Roman armies destroyed the temple in AD 70 (compare Luke 21:20). Many also see a further fulfillment before Christ's return.

24:28.t: "Vultures": the KJV's "eagles"; the Greek aetos can mean either.

24:36.t: "Only My Father": some manuscripts add "nor the Son" (compare Mark 13:32); the KJV does not have these words here.

24:51.t: "Cut him to pieces": the KJV's "cut him asunder"; perhaps a figure for severe punishment.

25:15.t: "Talents": a talent was a large sum of money, about twenty years' wages for a laborer. The English word "talent", meaning a gift or ability, comes from this parable.

25:27.t: "Interest": the KJV's "usury", which in 1611 meant any interest.

26:6.t: "Simon the Leper": probably a man Jesus had healed. John 12:1-8 tells of a similar anointing by Mary of Bethany.

26:7.t: "Perfume": the KJV's "ointment"; Mark 14:3 calls it pure nard. "Reclining at the table": the KJV's "as he sat at meat". At formal meals guests lay on couches around a low table.

26:15.t: "Thirty pieces of silver": probably silver shekels or tetradrachms, the price of a slave (Exodus 21:32). See Zechariah 11:12-13.

26:53.t: "Twelve legions": a Roman legion had about six thousand soldiers.

26:55.t: "Leading a rebellion": the KJV's "as against a thief"; Greek lestes, a robber or rebel.

26:59.t: "The whole Sanhedrin": the KJV's "all the council", the Jewish high court of seventy-one members.

26:64.t: "The Mighty One": the KJV's "power", a reverent way of saying God. Jesus combines Psalm 110:1 and Daniel 7:13.
"You have said so" (Greek su eipas): a guarded yes, "Those are your words." Jesus then claims far more, the place at God's right hand.

26:73.t: Galileans spoke with a distinct accent.

27:2.t: "Pilate": the KJV's "Pontius Pilate", the Roman governor of Judea from AD 26 to 36. Only Rome could carry out an execution.

27:5.t: Acts 1:18 describes Judas's death differently; the two accounts may describe the same event from different sides.

27:9.t: The words are closest to Zechariah 11:12-13, but Matthew names Jeremiah, perhaps because they also draw on Jeremiah's purchase of a field and his visit to the potter (Jeremiah 18-19, 32:6-9).

27:16.t: Some manuscripts read "Jesus Barabbas" in verses 16-17.

27:27.t: "The Praetorium": the KJV's "the common hall", the governor's headquarters. "Company": a cohort of up to six hundred soldiers.

27:34.t: "Sour wine": the KJV's "vinegar"; many manuscripts read "wine". Wine mixed with gall or myrrh dulled pain.

27:35.t: "That it might be fulfilled ... cast lots": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts do not have these words. The quotation is Psalm 22:18 (compare John 19:24).

27:38.t: "Robbers": the KJV's "thieves"; Greek lestes, a robber or rebel; see 26:55.

27:45.t: "From noon until three in the afternoon": the KJV's "from the sixth hour ... unto the ninth hour".

27:51.t: The curtain separated the Holy Place from the Most Holy Place, where only the high priest entered once a year (Hebrews 9:3-12, 10:19-20).

27:62.t: "Preparation Day": the day before the Sabbath, when everything was made ready.

28:1.t: "After the Sabbath, at dawn on the first day of the week": early Sunday morning.

28:9.t: "Greetings": the KJV's "All hail"; Greek chairete, "rejoice", the usual greeting.

28:20.t: "Amen": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts do not have it.
"The end of the age" (Greek synteleia tou aionos): the KJV's "the end of the world". The Greek aion means an age, not the physical world. See 13:39.

1:21.t: "Jesus" (Greek Iesous, from Hebrew Yeshua or Joshua): the name means "the LORD saves", which is why the angel says, "because He will save His people from their sins."

1:23.t: "The virgin" (Greek parthenos): Matthew quotes Isaiah 7:14 from the Greek translation, made before Christ, which rendered the Hebrew almah, a young woman of marriageable age never used in the Bible of a married woman, as parthenos, "virgin". See the note at Isaiah 7:14.

2:2.t: "Worship" (Greek proskuneo): to bow down before someone, used of honoring a king and of worshiping God. Matthew uses it often of people coming to Jesus (8:2, 14:33, 28:9, 28:17).

2:23.t: "He would be called a Nazarene": no Old Testament verse says this exactly. Matthew likely plays on the Hebrew netser, "branch" (Isaiah 11:1), and on the humble reputation of Nazareth (John 1:46).

3:2.t: "Repent" (Greek metanoeo): literally "to change one's mind", a turning of the whole life back to God, not only feeling sorry. It reflects the Hebrew shuv, "to return".

"The kingdom of heaven": Matthew's usual phrase for what Mark and Luke call "the kingdom of God". Out of reverence, Jews often said "heaven" in place of God's name. The kingdom is God's reign, now breaking into the world through Jesus.

3:6.t: "Baptized" (Greek baptizo): to dip or immerse in water. John's baptism was a sign of repentance and cleansing.

3:17.t: "My Son, whom I love" (Greek ho huios mou ho agapetos): the KJV's "my beloved Son". The words echo Psalm 2:7 and Isaiah 42:1. Agapetos, "beloved", is from agape, love that is not mainly a feeling but committed goodwill that seeks another's good, even an enemy's; the New Testament uses agape for God's love in Christ; see 5:44.

4:1.t: "Tempted" (Greek peirazo): to test or to tempt. The devil tempted Jesus to sin; God allowed the test to prove Him faithful where Israel had failed in the wilderness.

4:23.t: "Good news" (Greek euangelion): the KJV's "gospel". The word was used of royal announcements, such as a victory or the birth of an heir.

5:3.t: "Blessed" (Greek makarios): happy, fortunate, in God's favor. These sayings are called the Beatitudes, from the Latin beatus, "blessed". They describe the people who belong to God's kingdom.
"Poor in spirit": those who know their spiritual need and depend wholly on God, echoing Isaiah 61:1 and 66:2.

5:5.t: "The meek" (Greek praeis): not weak but gentle, humble, not grasping. Psalm 37:11 is the source. Jesus calls Himself "gentle" with the same word (11:29).

5:17.t: "Fulfill" (Greek pleroo): to fill up, complete, bring to full meaning. Jesus does not set the Law aside; He brings out its full intent and accomplishes what it pointed to.

5:32.t: "Sexual immorality" (Greek porneia): the KJV's "fornication", a broad word for sexual sin, here unfaithfulness in marriage.

5:43.t: "Love" (Greek agapao, the verb of agape): not mainly a feeling but committed goodwill that seeks another's good, even an enemy's. The New Testament uses agape for God's love in Christ (John 3:16, Romans 5:8, 1 John 4:8). Phileo, the other common verb, means the warm affection of friends; see John 21:15, where the two words appear side by side. "Hate your enemy" is not in the Law; it was a popular conclusion drawn from Leviticus 19:18.

5:48.t: "Perfect" (Greek teleios): complete, mature, whole. In context it means loving fully as God does, including enemies, not sinless perfection.

6:9.t: "Our Father" (Greek pater, likely Aramaic abba behind it): Jesus teaches His followers to speak to God as children to a father. "May Your name be kept holy": the KJV's "Hallowed be thy name". To hallow (Greek hagiazo) is to treat as holy.

6:11.t: "Daily" (Greek epiousios): a rare word whose meaning is uncertain: "needed for today", "for the coming day", or "necessary for life". Each reading trusts God for each day's need.

6:12.t: "Debts ... sins": Jesus calls sins "debts" (Greek opheilemata), echoing the Aramaic hoba, which means both. Verses 14-15 use paraptoma, "trespass" or "false step".

6:14.t: "Debts ... sins": Jesus calls sins "debts" (Greek opheilemata), echoing the Aramaic hoba, which means both. Verses 14-15 use paraptoma, "trespass" or "false step".

6:22.t: "Healthy ... unhealthy" (Greek haplous ... poneros): the KJV's "single ... evil". Haplous means single, sound, or generous; "an evil eye" was a Jewish idiom for stinginess (Deuteronomy 15:9). In context Jesus is speaking of a generous versus a grasping heart toward money.

6:25.t: "Do not worry" (Greek merimnao): the KJV's "take no thought", which in 1611 meant "do not be anxious". It does not mean not to plan.

7:1.t: "Do not judge" (Greek krino): often quoted to forbid any moral judgment. In context Jesus forbids hypocritical, condemning judgment; verses 5-6 and 15-20 still call for discernment.

7:23.t: "I never knew you" (Greek ginosko): to know personally, in relationship, not merely to know about. Compare John 10:14 and 2 Timothy 2:19.

8:20.t: "The Son of Man": Jesus' favorite name for Himself. It can simply mean "a human being" (Psalm 8:4), but it also recalls the heavenly "one like a son of man" who receives an everlasting kingdom (Daniel 7:13-14). Jesus uses it of His humility, His suffering and His coming glory.

8:29.t: "Torture us before the appointed time": the demons know a day of judgment is coming for them.

9:22.t: "Healed" (Greek sozo): the same word means "saved". The woman was healed in body and also restored, made whole, by her faith.

9:36.t: "He had compassion" (Greek splanchnizomai): literally "to be moved in one's inner parts", a deep, gut-level compassion. In the Gospels it is used only of Jesus and of figures in His parables who represent God.

10:2.t: "Apostles" (Greek apostolos): "one who is sent", a messenger with authority to act for the sender. Jesus sends the twelve in 10:5 (apostello).

10:16.t: "Shrewd ... innocent" (Greek phronimos ... akeraios): wise and alert to danger, yet pure and unmixed with evil.

10:28.t: "Soul" (Greek psyche): the life or inner self, which human killers cannot touch. "Hell" is geenna, Gehenna, from the Hebrew Ge-Hinnom, the Valley of Hinnom south of Jerusalem, where children had once been burned to Molech; it became the name for the place of final judgment; see 5:22. In 10:39 the same word psyche is translated "life".

10:38.t: "Take up their cross": a condemned man carried the crossbeam to his execution. Following Jesus means being ready to die to self, and even to die for Him.

11:12.t: "Has been subjected to violence, and violent people have been seizing it" (Greek biazetai ... biastai): a hard verse. It may mean the kingdom has suffered attack from violent opponents, or that the kingdom is forcefully advancing and eager people are pressing into it (compare Luke 16:16).

11:23.t: "Hades": the KJV's "hell". Hades (Hebrew Sheol) is the realm of the dead, not Gehenna, the place of final judgment (5:22). Here it pictures Capernaum's fall from pride, echoing Isaiah 14:13-15.

11:28.t: "Rest" (Greek anapausis): relief and refreshment. "Yoke": a rabbi's teaching was called his yoke. Jesus' yoke is "easy" (chrestos, kind, well-fitting), unlike the heavy burdens of the Pharisees' traditions (23:4). "Gentle" is praus, the same word as "meek" in 5:5.

12:31.t: "Blasphemy against the Spirit": in context, the Pharisees saw the Spirit's plain work in Jesus and called it Satan's. To reject the Spirit's witness to Jesus deliberately and finally is to refuse the only source of forgiveness. Those who fear they have committed it show by their concern that they have not.

12:36.t: "Careless" (Greek argos): idle, useless, not just wicked words. Words reveal the heart (12:34).

12:37.t: "Acquitted" (Greek dikaioo): the KJV's "justified", to be declared righteous in court. Paul uses the same word for God's verdict of righteousness on those who believe (Romans 3:24-28).

13:3.t: "Parables" (Greek parabole, Hebrew mashal): a story or comparison placed beside a truth to illuminate it. Jesus' parables reveal the kingdom to those willing to hear and conceal it from those who refuse (13:11-13).

13:11.t: "Mysteries" (Greek mysterion): not a puzzle but a secret once hidden and now revealed by God. Compare Romans 16:25-26.

13:21.t: "Fall away" (Greek skandalizo): the KJV's "is offended". The word means to trip over a snare or stumbling block. In 13:57 "took offense" is the same word.

13:58.t: "Lack of faith" (Greek apistia): Jesus' power was not limited, but He did not force miracles on people who refused to trust Him.

14:27.t: "It is I" (Greek ego eimi): literally "I am". It can be an ordinary "it is me", but on the lips of one walking on the sea it echoes God's name, "I AM" (Exodus 3:14, Isaiah 43:10-11). Only God walks on the waves of the sea (Job 9:8).

15:11.t: "Defile" (Greek koinoo): to make common or ceremonially unclean. Jesus moves purity from outward ritual to the heart. Mark 7:19 draws the conclusion that He declared all foods clean.

15:26.t: "Dogs" (Greek kynarion): "little dogs", house pets rather than street dogs. Jews sometimes called Gentiles dogs. Jesus tests the woman, and her humble, persistent faith wins His praise (15:28).

16:18.t: "You are Peter, and on this rock" (Greek Petros ... petra): a play on words. Petros means "stone", petra "rock"; in Aramaic both are kepha (Cephas). Christians differ on whether the rock is Peter himself, Peter's confession of faith, or Christ, whom Peter confessed. "Church" (Greek ekklesia): an assembly of people called out, used in the Greek Old Testament for the congregation of Israel. "Gates of Hades": the power of death. Hades (Hebrew Sheol) is the realm of the dead, not Gehenna, the place of final judgment; see 11:23.

16:19.t: "Bind ... loose": rabbinic terms for forbidding and permitting, or for declaring sins retained or forgiven (compare 18:18, John 20:23). The Greek tense can be read "will have been bound in heaven", meaning that the apostles declare what heaven has already decided.

16:25.t: "Life ... soul" (Greek psyche): the same word in both verses. To gain everything and lose one's psyche is to lose one's very self.

17:2.t: "Transfigured" (Greek metamorphoo): changed in form. Jesus' hidden glory shone through. Paul uses the same word for believers being transformed (Romans 12:2, 2 Corinthians 3:18).

18:3.t: "Change" (Greek strepho): the KJV's "be converted", to turn around. Children depend wholly on others and claim no status; so must those who enter the kingdom.

18:6.t: "Stumble" (Greek skandalizo): to trip over a snare or stumbling block, to be led into sin or to fall away; see 13:21. "A large millstone": literally "a donkey's millstone", one turned by a donkey, far heavier than a hand mill.

18:17.t: "Church" (Greek ekklesia): an assembly of people called out, used in the Greek Old Testament for the congregation of Israel; see 16:18. Here it means the local gathering of believers.

18:27.t: "Canceled the debt" (Greek aphiemi): the same word means to forgive, to release, to let go. The parable makes forgiving debts a picture of forgiving sins (6:12).

19:24.t: "The eye of a needle": a deliberate exaggeration. A story that a gate in Jerusalem was called "the Needle's Eye" has no ancient evidence. Salvation is impossible by human effort, possible only with God (19:26).

19:28.t: "The renewal of all things" (Greek palingenesia): the KJV's "the regeneration", the new birth of the whole creation at the end of the age. Paul uses the same word for personal new birth (Titus 3:5).

20:15.t: "Are you envious because I am generous?" (Greek ho ophthalmos sou poneros estin): literally "Is your eye evil because I am good?" "An evil eye" was a Jewish idiom for stinginess or envy (Deuteronomy 15:9); see 6:22-23.

20:28.t: "Ransom" (Greek lytron): the price paid to free a slave or prisoner. "For many" (Greek anti pollon): "in place of many", echoing the Servant who bears the sin of many (Isaiah 53:11-12).

21:9.t: "Hosanna" (Hebrew hoshia na, Psalm 118:25): "Save, please!" By Jesus' time it was also a shout of praise. "Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord" is from Psalm 118:26.

21:19.t: The fig tree is an acted parable. Leaves without fruit picture Israel's leaders, outwardly religious but fruitless (compare Jeremiah 8:13, Micah 7:1).

22:21.t: "Image" (Greek eikon): the coin bore Caesar's image, so it belonged to him. Humans bear God's image (Genesis 1:27), so they belong to God.

23:7.t: "Rabbi" (Hebrew rabbi): "my great one", a title of respect for a teacher. Jesus forbids not respect for teachers but status-seeking: all His followers are equals under one Teacher.

23:33.t: "Condemned to hell" (Greek krisis tes geennes): the KJV's "the damnation of hell". "Damnation" in 1611 meant condemnation or judgment. Gehenna is Gehenna, from the Hebrew Ge-Hinnom, the Valley of Hinnom south of Jerusalem, where children had once been burned to Molech; it became the name for the place of final judgment; see 5:22.

24:8.t: "Birth pains" (Greek odin): the KJV's "sorrows". The troubles are not the end but the labor pains that come before a new age.

24:34.t: "This generation" (Greek genea): readers disagree. Some take it as Jesus' contemporaries, who saw Jerusalem fall in AD 70; others as the generation alive when the final signs appear, or as "this kind of people".

25:31.t: "The least of these brothers and sisters of Mine" (Greek adelphoi): readers differ on whether this means any person in need or Jesus' disciples in particular (compare 10:40-42, 12:49-50). Either way, how people treat those Jesus identifies with is how they treat Him.

25:46.t: "Eternal punishment ... eternal life" (Greek kolasis aionios ... zoe aionios): the same adjective aionios, "eternal", "of the age to come", describes both.

26:26.t: "This is My body": Christians differ on how Christ is present in the Lord's Supper: as a real presence in the bread and wine, as a spiritual presence, or as a memorial sign. All agree that Jesus gave the meal to be repeated in memory of His death (1 Corinthians 11:23-26).

26:28.t: "Covenant" (Greek diatheke): the KJV's "testament". Diatheke can mean a will or testament, but here it translates the Hebrew berit, covenant. Jesus' words echo the blood of the covenant at Sinai (Exodus 24:8) and the new covenant promised in Jeremiah 31:31-34. "Forgiveness" (Greek aphesis): the KJV's "remission", release from a debt; the related verb aphiemi means to forgive, to release, to let go, and the parable of 18:23-35 makes forgiving debts a picture of forgiving sins (see 18:27).

26:39.t: "This cup": in the prophets the cup often stands for God's wrath poured out on sin (Isaiah 51:17, Jeremiah 25:15). Jesus shrinks from it, yet submits to the Father's will.

26:41.t: "The spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak" (Greek pneuma ... sarx): the disciples' desire is real, but human nature is frail. Sarx, "flesh", here means human nature with its weakness, not sinful nature as in some of Paul's letters (see John 1:14).

27:46.t: "Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani?" (Hebrew and Aramaic): the opening line of Psalm 22, which moves from forsakenness to trust and ends in praise. Jesus truly bore the separation of sin (2 Corinthians 5:21), and by quoting the psalm He pointed to its whole story.

27:50.t: "He gave up His spirit" (Greek apheken to pneuma): the KJV's "yielded up the ghost". Jesus' death is described as an act of His own, laying down His life (John 10:18).

27:54.t: "The Son of God": the Greek has no article and could be read "a son of God", as a pagan soldier might have meant. Matthew, however, presents his words as a confession of who Jesus truly is.

28:19.t: "Make disciples" (Greek matheteusate): the main command; "go", "baptizing" and "teaching" describe how it is done. "In the name" is singular: one name shared by Father, Son and Holy Spirit.
